title: Cranmer's hand
hookLine: after recanting, he recants his recantation and puts the hand that signed into the fire first
last: CLEANSE THE THOUGHTS OF OUR HEARTS.

lines: AN OLD MAN IN A CHURCH IN OXFORD.
HE HAS SIGNED IT ALL AWAY.
cards: An old man stands in a church in Oxford, in front of a crowd. He has been in prison a long time.
He is the archbishop who gave England its prayer book, and he has since signed papers taking it all back: accepting the pope, accepting the teaching he once argued against.
The crowd has been told what to expect: one more statement of regret, and then he will be burned anyway. He starts to speak. He asks for prayers.
He talks about the world, about money, about obeying the queen. Then he reaches his writings, and the speech goes somewhere nobody planned.

teach.b: Here's how he got there. When Henry's son Edward died, Mary became queen, Catherine of Aragon's daughter. She brought England back to the Catholic faith and under Rome.
Cranmer had declared her mother's marriage void.
He was tried for heresy and kept in prison, and under that pressure he signed recantations. Even so, he was sent to the stake.
The story of the end is told by John Foxe, a Protestant writer who collected the stories of those Mary burned. Foxe has a side, and readers weigh his telling with that in mind.
In Foxe's account, Cranmer says the papers he signed were written against the truth in his heart, out of fear of death.

Since his hand had offended by writing them, his hand would be punished first. At the stake, Foxe says, he stretched his right hand into the flames and held it there before the fire reached the rest of him.
Some readers think of Peter here. The night Jesus was arrested, Peter warmed himself at a fire and swore he didn't know him.
Then the rooster crowed, and in the King James Bible, "he went out, and wept bitterly." Later, by another fire on a beach, the risen Jesus gave him a way back.
Protestants honor Cranmer as a martyr and the voice of the prayer book. Catholics remember the archbishop who helped break England from Rome.
Either way, the story ends with a frightened man who, at the very end, stopped hiding what he thought.

how: Anglicans and other Protestants remember Thomas Cranmer as a martyr and as the main shaper of the Book of Common Prayer, and the story of his hand in the fire is often retold from Foxe's Book of Martyrs.

o: a hand raised to swear loyalty to the queen
the hand that signed, held first in the fire

p: signed in prison, out of fear
the Protestant writer who told the story

s: he signed recantations in prison, then took them back at the end.
signing the recantations saved his life
even so, he was still sent to the stake.
the well-known scene comes to us from a writer with a side
John Foxe was a Protestant writer, and readers weigh his telling with that in mind.

games.q: you're Cranmer, brought out to read one last statement of regret before you're burned. what do you do?
o: take back the recantations and say why.
refuse to say anything at all.
games.why: in Foxe's account, he takes them back: they were written out of fear of death, so the hand that wrote them will be punished first.

practice: This isn't about punishing yourself. Look at your own hand and let it bring something to mind, a message it typed, a thing it signed, a door it shut, and name the mistake in one plain sentence, no excuses attached.
Then let your hand rest open; if you pray, hand it to God that way, and if you don't, notice what it's like to say it straight.

wordCard.voice: Cranmer's hand. The hand that signed his recantations, which, in John Foxe's account, he held in the fire first, owning his mistake before he died.

carryVoice: Your line: this hand first. Even a frightened person can stop hiding. See you tomorrow.
